skill.name: Two good edits: which suits this reader better?
skill.why: Good writing fits its reader. The same news needs different words for different people.
skill.how: Ask who's reading and why. Pick the edit that gives them what they need.

beats.say: Sometimes two edits are both good writing.
beats.show: Edit A: **The lava is very hot.** Edit B: **Lava can reach 1,200 °C.**

beats.say: So ask: who is going to read it?
A five-year-old needs short, simple words.
A science report needs exact facts.
Pick the edit that gives this reader what they need.

weDo.text:
Wren is writing a note that a teacher will read to a five-year-old, who will feed the newsroom fish.

Edit A: Give the fish one pinch of food. Just one!
Edit B: Sprinkle a small quantity of flakes, as overfeeding fouls the water.
weDo.prompt: Which edit suits the five-year-old better, and why?
weDo.hint: Who is reading? Which edit would a five-year-old understand?
weDo.success: Edit A uses short, everyday words and tells the child exactly what to do.

options.text: Edit A: its words are easy and it gives one clear amount.
Edit A: it ends with an exclamation mark, so it sounds fun.
options.reason: It does sound fun, but a fun mark won't help a child feed fish. Look at the words.

options.text: Edit B: it explains why, and a reason helps a rule stick.
options.reason: A reason can help, but a five-year-old won't know 'quantity' or 'overfeeding'.

weDo.prompt: Tap the edit that suits the council better.
weDo.hint: What does the council need so it can act: a feeling, or facts?
weDo.success: Edit B tells the council which drains, where, and for how long. That's what it needs to act.

parts:
Gus is writing to the council about the smelly drains. The council needs facts so it can decide what to fix.

Edit A:

parts.tap: The drains smell so bad that my eyebrows curled.
parts.reason: It's funny, but a feeling doesn't tell the council what to fix.

parts.tap: Six drains on Lava Street have smelt bad for three weeks.
Please, please fix the drains before the whole town faints.
parts.reason: It's a strong plea, but it gives no facts about which drains or for how long.

creature.name: Suitrel
creature.blurb: A nankeen kestrel that hovers over the volcano's slopes, studying who is below. Only when it knows its reader does it dive with the right words.

encounters.frame: Wren is making a sign for the gecko tank. Suitrel is hovering over two edits.
encounters.text:
The sign is for the kinder kids who visit the newsroom. They are five years old.

Edit A: Please be gentle with the gecko. Pat his back with one finger.
Edit B: Handle the gecko with care, as stress harms reptiles.
encounters.prompt: Which edit suits the five-year-olds better, and why?
encounters.success: Edit A is longer, but its words are easy, and it shows the kids exactly how to pat him.

options.text: Edit B, because it is shorter, so little kids can follow it more easily.
options.reason: It is shorter, but kinder kids won't know 'stress' or 'reptiles'.

options.text: Edit A, because it shows them how to pat him, in easy words.
Edit A, because it has two sentences instead of one.
options.reason: True, but more sentences don't help by themselves. Look for words a five-year-old knows.

encounters.frame: Gus wrote his space facts two ways. Suitrel needs to know who each one is for.
encounters.prompt: Match each edit to the reader it suits better.
encounters.success: Little kids need everyday words and fun comparisons. Space Club readers want exact facts and science words.

items.text: Mars is red because its dust is rusty, like an old bike left in the rain.
items.reason: It's long, but every word is one a four-year-old knows, and the bike helps him picture it.

items.text: Mars looks red because of iron oxide dust.
items.reason: 'Iron oxide' is a science term. It suits Space Club readers.

items.text: The Sun is a really, really big star.
items.reason: 'Really, really big' is how you'd explain it to a little kid.

items.text: The Sun is a star about 1.4 million km wide.
items.reason: An exact number suits a fact sheet for Space Club.

items.text: Whoosh! A rocket gobbles up its fuel like a very hungry dragon.
items.reason: Whoosh and a hungry dragon are fun for a four-year-old. A fact sheet needs exact facts.

encounters.frame: Suitrel is watching Tully write a note to her coach.
encounters.prompt: Tap the edit that suits the coach better.
encounters.success: Edit C gives the score, which is exactly what the coach needs to know.

parts:
The coach was sick and missed the game. The coach needs to know the score.

Edit A:

parts.tap: We won, and Mia took a great mark in the last quarter.
parts.reason: It's a great detail, but it still doesn't tell the coach the score.

parts.tap: We won, and it was the best day ever!
parts.reason: It shares a feeling, but the coach needs to know the score.

parts.tap: We won 58 to 46, and I kicked three goals.

encounters.frame: Zed is writing to his gran about his new game. Gran has never played a video game.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence Gran won't understand, then choose the edit that suits her.
encounters.success: 'I beat the hardest part' uses everyday words, so Gran can enjoy Zed's win too.

parts.tap: Dear Gran,
parts.reason: A friendly greeting suits Gran. Keep it.

parts.tap: I got a new game for my birthday.
parts.reason: Gran knows all these words, so this suits her.

parts.tap: I speedran the boss with no hits.
It was so much fun.
parts.reason: Gran will understand this. Keep it.

options.text: I no-hit the boss on hard mode.
options.reason: 'No-hit' and 'hard mode' are gamer words. Gran won't know them.

options.text: I beat the hardest part without a scratch.
I got a new PB on the boss fight.
options.reason: 'PB' and 'boss fight' are gamer words Gran won't know.

encounters.frame: Indi is making a sign for the newsroom door. Suitrel is hovering over two edits.
encounters.text:
People rush past this door all day. They only have time for a quick glance.

Edit A: Wet paint. Please don't touch.
Edit B: We painted this door this morning, so it may still be wet. Please don't touch it.
encounters.prompt: Which edit suits people rushing past, and why?
encounters.success: Edit A says the important part in five words, so rushing readers get it at a glance.

options.text: Edit B, because it says when the door was painted.
options.reason: That's true, but people rushing past won't stop to read it all.

options.text: Edit B, because it uses full sentences, like a proper notice.
options.reason: True, but people rushing past only have time for a glance.

options.text: Edit A, because the warning is only five words long.

encounters.frame: Indi is writing a line for the kinder class song sheet. Suitrel is listening.
encounters.prompt: Tap the edit that suits the four-year-olds better.
encounters.success: Bang, shake, drums and bells are words four-year-olds know and can act out.

parts:
Their teacher will read the line aloud to four-year-olds.

Edit A:

parts.tap: Follow the conductor and keep a steady tempo.
parts.reason: 'Conductor' and 'tempo' are words for older music students, not four-year-olds.

parts.tap: Let's bang the drums and shake the bells!
Today we will explore rhythm using percussion instruments.
parts.reason: 'Rhythm' and 'percussion' are words for older readers, not four-year-olds.

encounters.frame: Mo is writing a label for the cake stall. Suitrel is checking who it's for.
encounters.text:
This label is for kids with a nut allergy. They need to know if the cake is safe to eat.

Edit A: Gooey chocolate cake with a crunchy golden topping.
Edit B: Chocolate cake with a peanut topping. Not safe for nut allergies.
encounters.prompt: Which edit suits these readers better, and why?
encounters.success: Kids with a nut allergy need to know about the peanuts. Edit B tells them clearly.

options.text: Edit A, because it tells readers what the topping is like.
options.reason: It does, but 'crunchy golden' doesn't say what the topping is made of.

options.text: Edit B, because it says the cake has peanuts in it.
Edit A, because 'gooey' and 'crunchy' make it sound tasty.
options.reason: Tasty words won't keep a kid with a nut allergy safe.

encounters.frame: Wren is reading her news on the island radio. Suitrel is listening in.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't suit radio listeners, then choose a better edit.
encounters.success: Listeners can't see a photo, but they can picture a surfboard. The words show the size.

parts: Radio listeners can hear Wren, but they can't see any pictures.

parts.tap: Good morning, Redpen Volcano!
parts.reason: A cheery hello works well on the radio. Keep it.

parts.tap: A sea turtle swam into the steaming bay this week.
parts.reason: Listeners can picture this from the words alone.

parts.tap: As you can see in this photo, it is huge.
Rangers say it is healthy and happy.
parts.reason: This works on the radio. It doesn't need a picture.

options.text: It is as long as a surfboard.
Just look at the size of it in this photo!
options.reason: Radio listeners can't see a photo, so they still won't know how big it is.

options.text: This picture shows just how big it is.
options.reason: There are no pictures on the radio. Listeners need words that show the size.

encounters.frame: Gus wrote his slime lines two ways. Suitrel is sorting out who each line is for.
encounters.prompt: Match each line to the reader it suits better.
encounters.success: Judges want science words, methods and results. A six-year-old wants everyday words, fun comparisons and gross details.

items.text: Slime stretches because it's full of long, wiggly strings, a bit like a bowl of spaghetti.
items.reason: It explains the science, but with everyday words and a fun comparison that suit a six-year-old.

items.text: Slime is a polymer: long chains of molecules that slide past each other.
items.reason: 'Polymer' and 'molecules' are science words that judges expect.

items.text: Method: we measured each stretch in centimetres.
items.reason: It's short, but judges want to know the method and how the test was measured.

items.text: The green slime smelt like old socks! Yuck!
items.reason: A silly, gross detail is perfect for a six-year-old.

items.text: Our results show that more glue made the slime stretch further.
items.reason: Judges want the results of the experiment.

encounters.frame: Zed is writing a welcome note for his cousin Lily. Suitrel is hovering over two edits.
encounters.prompt: Tap the edit that suits Lily better.
encounters.success: Lily is scared, so she needs to feel safe. Edit C explains the creaks and comforts her.

parts:
Lily is seven. She is staying in the old lava-tube cabin, and she is scared of the dark.

Edit A:

parts.tap: The cabin was built by miners over a hundred years ago.
parts.reason: It's interesting history, but it doesn't help a scared seven-year-old feel safe.

parts.tap: The cabin creaks at night. Some say it's the ghost of an old miner.
parts.reason: It's a great spooky line, but it would scare Lily even more.

parts.tap: The cabin creaks at night, but that's just the wind. You're safe here.

encounters.frame: Tully is writing for the Reef Rays match program. Suitrel is reading over her shoulder.
encounters.text:
The program is for fans who missed last week's game. They want to know what happened.

Edit A: Last week, the Rays beat the Crabs by twelve points in the pouring rain.
Edit B: Last week, I felt so proud of my team that I could have burst!
encounters.prompt: Which edit suits these fans better, and why?
encounters.success: Edit A tells fans who won and by how much. That's what someone who missed the game needs.

options.text: Edit A, because it says who won and by how much.
Edit A, because it mentions the pouring rain.
options.reason: The rain is a nice detail, but it isn't what fans who missed the game need most.

options.text: Edit B, because fans love to share the excitement of a win with the writer.
options.reason: That can be fun, but fans who missed the game need to know who won first.

encounters.frame: Gus is writing instructions for the newsroom robot. Suitrel is circling the desk.
encounters.prompt: Tap the edit that suits Grandpa Ray better.
encounters.success: Edit B uses everyday words and tells Grandpa Ray exactly what he'll see and hear.

parts:
The instructions are for Grandpa Ray, who has never used a robot or a phone app.

Edit A:

parts.tap: Long-press the power key, then follow the on-screen setup.
parts.reason: 'Long-press' and 'on-screen setup' are for people who have used gadgets before.

parts.tap: Press the big green button on its chest. It will say hello.
Boot it from the chest panel, then pair it with the app.
parts.reason: 'Boot', 'pair' and 'app' are tech words Grandpa Ray won't know.

encounters.frame: Indi is writing to the council about the crater path. Suitrel is hovering over two edits.
encounters.text:
Indi wants the council to fix the crater path. Councillors want facts they can check and act on.

Edit A: The path is so terrible that I nearly cried the last time I walked on it.
Edit B: Twelve steps on the path are cracked, and two people tripped there last week.
encounters.prompt: Which edit suits the council better, and why?
encounters.success: Cracked steps and people tripping are facts the council can check. That helps them decide.

options.text: Edit A, because it uses 'I', so it sounds like a real letter.
options.reason: True, but councillors need facts they can check, not how the letter sounds.

options.text: Edit B, because it is shorter and quicker to read.
options.reason: It is a little shorter, but that isn't what matters. What can councillors check?

options.text: Edit A, because it shows the council how serious the problem is for Indi.
options.reason: It shows how Indi feels, but councillors can't measure a feeling or know what to fix.

options.text: Edit B, because it counts the cracked steps and the people who tripped.

encounters.frame: Wren made a fact card for the kinder visit. Suitrel spotted a line that doesn't fit.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't suit five-year-olds, then choose the edit that does.
encounters.success: 'Eats bugs and plants' and 'loves lying on warm rocks' say the same thing in words five-year-olds know.

parts: A teacher will read this card aloud to five-year-olds.

parts.tap: Meet the bearded dragon!
parts.reason: A cheerful hello suits five-year-olds. Keep it.

parts.tap: It has spikes under its chin.
parts.reason: Simple words that are easy to picture. This suits them.

parts.tap: It is an ectothermic omnivore.
Would you like to hold one?
parts.reason: A friendly question suits young listeners. Keep it.

options.text: It is a cold-blooded reptile with an omnivorous diet.
options.reason: 'Cold-blooded' and 'omnivorous' are words five-year-olds won't know.

options.text: It eats bugs and plants and loves lying on warm rocks.
Scientists class it as an ectotherm and an omnivore.
options.reason: That's correct, but 'ectotherm' and 'omnivore' are too hard for five-year-olds.

options.text: It regulates its temperature by basking in sunlight.
options.reason: 'Regulates' and 'temperature' are words five-year-olds won't know.

encounters.frame: Indi wrote lines about her lava mural for two different readers. Suitrel is sorting them.
encounters.prompt: Match each line to the reader it suits better.
encounters.success: Judges want art words, materials and exact details. Young kids want everyday words and fun things to spot.

bins: Year 2 kids on a school tour

items.text: Indi layered thin glazes of acrylic paint to make the lava glow.
items.reason: Judges want to know the technique, and 'glazes' is an art word.

items.text: Indi painted the lava in lots of thin, see-through layers, so it glows like a night light.
items.reason: It explains how she did it, but in everyday words with a comparison Year 2 kids know.

items.text: Can you spot the tiny goat hiding on the rock?
items.reason: A spot-it question is fun for young kids on a tour.

items.text: Acrylic on plywood, 2 metres by 3 metres.
items.reason: It's short, but the materials and exact size are details judges look for.

items.text: The brushstrokes get shorter and faster near the crater, adding a sense of movement.
items.reason: This explains the technique and its effect, which judges look for.

encounters.frame: Zed is writing a help page for Lava Leap. Suitrel is hovering over two edits.
encounters.prompt: Tap the edit that suits brand-new players better.
encounters.success: Edit A explains each move in plain words, so someone who has never played can follow it.

parts:
The help page is for brand-new players. Most of them have never played a jumping game before.

Edit A:

parts.tap: Tap the screen to jump. Hold your finger down to jump higher.
Spam-tap to bunny-hop, then chain a charged jump over the gap.
parts.reason: Expert players would love this, but new players won't know 'spam-tap' or 'bunny-hop'.

parts.tap: Leap over rivers of lava and dodge fireballs on your way to the golden volcano!
parts.reason: It makes the game sound exciting, but it doesn't tell new players how to jump.

encounters.frame: Wren is writing a safety sign for the black-sand beach. Suitrel is circling overhead.
encounters.text:
The sign stands at the beach entrance. Swimmers read it as they walk past, about to go in.

Edit A: Strong rips. Swim between the flags.
Edit B: The ocean here hides powerful rip currents that have surprised even experienced swimmers.
encounters.prompt: Which edit suits these swimmers better, and why?
encounters.success: Swimmers walking past need the danger and the action fast. Edit A gives both in six words.

options.text: Edit B, because it uses the proper name, rip currents.
options.reason: True, but swimmers walking past need to know what to do, and fast.

options.text: Edit A, because two quick lines name the danger and the safe spot.
Edit A, because it has fewer hard words for little kids.
options.reason: True, but this sign is for swimmers of every age. Think about how fast they read it.

options.text: Edit B, because saying even experienced swimmers get caught makes people take it seriously.
options.reason: It might, but it never says what to do, and people walking past won't read it all.

encounters.frame: Indi is writing to the school music teacher for the Crater Kids band. Suitrel thinks one line misses.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't give Ms Vega what she needs, then choose a better edit.
encounters.success: Ms Vega needs two facts to choose bands. This edit gives both: the instruments and ten minutes.

parts: Ms Vega is choosing bands for the school concert. She needs to know what each band plays and how long its set is.

parts.tap: Dear Ms Vega,
parts.reason: A polite greeting suits a teacher. Keep it.

parts.tap: The Crater Kids would love to play at the school concert.
parts.reason: This says what the band wants. Ms Vega needs that too.

parts.tap: Our music makes people want to dance on the tables!
Thank you for thinking about us.
parts.reason: A polite thank-you suits a teacher. Keep it.

options.text: Everyone who hears us says we're the best band on the island.
options.reason: That's praise, but Ms Vega needs the instruments and how long you'll play.

options.text: Our songs are about lava, goats and Mo's terrible cooking.
options.reason: It's fun, but it doesn't tell her the instruments or the set length.

options.text: We play guitar, drums and keyboard, and our set is ten minutes long.
We would be honoured to play for your wonderful students.
options.reason: It's polite, but it still doesn't say the instruments or the set length.

encounters.frame: Gus is writing the permission note for the night trip to the observatory. Suitrel is hovering over two edits.
encounters.text:
The note goes home to parents. It must tell them everything they need to say yes and get their child ready for the trip.

Edit A: Students will spend an unforgettable night at the volcano observatory, watching a meteor shower through real telescopes.
Edit B: The trip runs from 7 pm to 10 pm on Friday 12 June. It costs $15, and students need a warm jacket.
encounters.prompt: Which edit suits the parents better, and why?
encounters.success: A permission note is for planning. Edit B tells parents when, how much and what to pack.

options.text: Edit A, because parents are more likely to say yes when the trip sounds worthwhile.
options.reason: It might help, but parents can't sign or pack without the date, the hours and the cost.

options.text: Edit A, because it names the place, the volcano observatory.
options.reason: True, but naming the place isn't enough. Parents still need to plan the night.

options.text: Edit B, because it covers the date, the hours, the price and the jacket.
Edit B, because its numbers make the note look official.
options.reason: Looking official isn't the point. Think about what parents must do before they say yes.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote about the same snake for three different readers. Suitrel is sorting the lines.
encounters.text: Wren saw a red-bellied black snake on the basalt ridge. She wrote lines for three readers: a ranger's field report, a sign for hikers on the path and a picture book for preschoolers.
encounters.prompt: Match each line to the reader it suits best.
encounters.success: Rangers need exact records, hikers need quick instructions and preschoolers need a gentle story.

items.text: SNAKE AREA. If you meet a snake, stop, stay still and let it move away.
items.reason: A path sign needs a clear warning and short instructions for hikers.

items.text: Sammy the snake slid under a warm, flat rock for a long afternoon nap, and nobody woke him up.
items.reason: A named snake and a cosy nap make a gentle story for preschoolers.

items.text: One adult, about 1.2 metres long, was sighted at 9.20 am on the eastern scree slope.
items.reason: Exact length, time and place are what a field report records.

items.text: Snakes rest on these rocks in summer. Please keep to the path.
items.reason: It warns hikers and tells them what to do, in two short sentences.

items.text: Second sighting: two adults, basking, 40 min.
items.reason: It's short, but exact counts and times in note form suit a ranger's records.

encounters.frame: Gus is writing the leaflet for the Stinking Vents walk. Suitrel thinks one sentence misses its readers.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't help these readers, then choose the edit that does.
encounters.success: Visitors with asthma need to know how to stay safe. This edit tells them exactly what to do.

parts: This leaflet is for visitors with asthma. They need to know whether the walk is safe for them and what to do.

parts.tap: The Stinking Vents are on the eastern side of Redpen Volcano, a twenty-minute walk from the car park.
parts.reason: Visitors need to know where the vents are and how far they'll walk.

parts.tap: The vents release sulphur gas, which can make breathing harder for people with asthma.
parts.reason: This tells visitors with asthma about the risk. It's exactly what they need.

parts.tap: Over a thousand years, the gas has stained the rocks a brilliant, buttery yellow.
If your chest feels tight, move upwind at once and return to the car park.
parts.reason: This tells them what to do if they feel unwell. Keep it.

options.text: At sunset, the yellow rocks glow like gold against the dark crater walls.
options.reason: It's a lovely picture, but it doesn't help someone with asthma stay safe.

options.text: The vents were first mapped by a team of rock scientists in 1962.
options.reason: It's a history fact, but it doesn't help visitors with asthma stay safe.

options.text: People with asthma should carry their puffer and stay behind the yellow rope.
Some of these vents have been puffing out gas since long before people lived here.
options.reason: It's an interesting fact, but it doesn't help visitors with asthma stay safe.

encounters.frame: Tully is writing the footy club's request to the council. Suitrel is hovering over two edits.
encounters.prompt: Tap the edit that suits the council better.
encounters.success: Edit C gives a number and a reason, so the council can see who the lights would help.

parts:
The council is deciding whether to pay for lights at the oval. Councillors want to know how many people the lights would help.

Edit A:

parts.tap: There is nothing quite like the roar of a crowd under bright lights on a cold winter night.
parts.reason: It's a vivid line, but it doesn't tell the council how many people the lights would help.

parts.tap: Ours is the only oval in town without lights, so every night game is played somewhere else.
parts.reason: It's a useful fact, but it doesn't tell the council how many people the lights would help.

parts.tap: Lights would let our 140 junior players train after school all winter, when it is dark by 5.30 pm.

encounters.frame: Mo's goat, Pebbles, ate the neighbour's fence. Mo is writing a note to say sorry.
encounters.text:
Mrs Flint next door is upset. She wants an apology, and she wants to know her fence will be fixed.

Edit A: Sorry about the fence! Pebbles thought it was a snack, but in her defence, it was a very tasty-looking fence.
Edit B: I'm sorry Pebbles ate your fence. I'll rebuild it on Saturday.
encounters.prompt: Which edit suits Mrs Flint better, and why?
encounters.success: Mrs Flint is upset, so a joke could backfire. Edit B says sorry and promises a repair.

options.text: Edit B, because it apologises plainly and names a day for the repair.
Edit A, because a little humour can soften an apology and help her smile.
options.reason: Mrs Flint is upset, and the joke makes light of her fence. It also promises no repair.

options.text: Edit B, because it is shorter, so she can read it quickly.
options.reason: It is shorter, but that isn't why it works. Think about what an upset neighbour wants.

options.text: Edit A, because it starts with sorry straight away.
options.reason: It does start with sorry, but then it jokes about her fence. What else does she want?

encounters.frame: Mo is writing a recipe for the Rumble's Cooking with Kids page. Suitrel is hovering over two edits.
encounters.prompt: Tap the edit that suits the young cooks better.
encounters.success: An eight-year-old shouldn't lift a hot tray alone. Edit A brings in an adult and oven mitts.

parts:
The page is for children aged eight, cooking with an adult. Safety comes first.

Edit A:

parts.tap: Ask an adult to lift the hot tray out of the oven, wearing thick oven mitts.
Remove the tray from the 220-degree oven and rest it on a heatproof trivet for ten minutes.
parts.reason: It's clear for adult cooks, but it tells an eight-year-old to handle a hot tray alone.

parts.tap: Take the tray out of the oven as soon as the top turns golden brown.
parts.reason: It says when, but it still has an eight-year-old take a hot tray out alone.
